news.title: Schumer reckoning imminent as posse of new senators circles: 'He's holding us back'
news.description: Progressives sending a posse of Democrats to the U.S. Senate in January have a message for Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY): Join us or get out of our way. Leaders from top progressive groups spoke out Thursday against the Democratic Party’s presumptive majority leader for a centrist stance that saw Schumer recently claim he’d work with Donald Trump, should the president be willing to change his ways. “We have to work to end the corruption that is poisoning our politics and our economy,” Jenifer Fernandez-Ancona, chief strategy officer of Way to Win, said Thursday. “You can’t run against a rigged system in November then compromise with the people who rigged it.” Adam Green, co-founder of Progressive Change Campaign Coalition, called out the ranking Democrat by name. “It’s a matter of leveraging the awesome people who just got elected and the fresh mandate they have to force Chuck Schumer to think bigger,” said Green. “We’re still moving, but he’s holding us back — and we need some cultural things to get him into shape.” Schumer, an establishment Democrat who often garners criticism for party-bucking compromises, will likely be elected in January to lead a host of senators with decidedly different perspectives on politics. Democrats who flipped their states on an economic populist platform include Troy Jackson in Maine, James Talarico in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Josh Turek in Iowa. They’ll be joined by progressive Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, and at least 12 Democrat colleagues who ran on an affordability policy platform that focused on corruption at the top. It was a gambit that worked, argued Fernandez-Ancona. "The lesson isn’t that Democrats need to abandon vulnerable people to win," she said. "It’s that we need to stop fighting elections on Republican terms." Data backs her claim. Populist Democrats who campaigned on fighting corruption and improving workers’ pay saw a 9-point gain on the generic message of protecting the Constitution and supporting economic growth, according to a recent poll conducted by Data for Progress. Executive Director Ryan O’Donnell added that nearly 30 percent of swing voters said they’d vote for Democrats who supported taxing the rich — 24 percent said they’d go blue for a Medicare for All healthcare system. Joel Payne, of MoveOn Political Action, argued Thursday that American voters sent a clear mandate to Washington to deliver funding to the Affordable Care Act and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and to end the war in Iran driving up gas prices. Should Democrats hope to reclaim the White House in 2028, argued Payne, they’ll need to deliver results on the promises they made — and he pointed to past election cycles as proof. “There was a crisis of trust in the grassroots of our party —people felt like they were sending leaders to Washington with a clear mandate and they were passing on doing the things,” Payne said. “Right now is the moment where folks want action and want leaders and leadership to be action-oriented. A good way to burn off the trust that you built on Election Day is to half-step and to back down.” Green, of the Progressive Change Campaign Coalition, argued that while incoming Democrats don’t have the votes to block Schumer’s appointment as majority leader, they still have the power to deliver results to the people. How? By taking aim at the filibuster. Roughly 40 Democrats and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) would likely throw their support behind fighting the filibuster — a Senate tactic that lets a minority of senators block or delay a vote on legislation by keeping debate going and preventing a bill from moving to a final vote — because of the gain it would win them. It would prevent a minority of Republicans from blocking Democratic bills from moving to a vote. “Getting rid of the filibuster gives us a clean story for the American public, as clean as Abdul El-Sayed, during the campaign trail, saying, ‘Money in your pocket, money out of politics, Medicare for all,’” argued Green. "When the House passes a minimum wage bill, is the story that the American people get going to be, “Minimum wage bill goes to Donald Trump’s desk and he either signs or vetoes it?” Or is it that we’re going to be talking about the Byrd Rule?" What's more, while Schumer might refuse to go along, such a demand would put him in a tight spot, Green argued. "If there is any chance of having oxygen in the room for a new Democratic leader, it is if someone broaches the question of filibuster reform and Chuck Schumer says no," Green said. "That immediately puts 40 Democrats and Sanders against him."

news.title: Fury brewing over Senator's 'blank check' written for a 'dirty' deal: 'Blatant disregard'
news.description: Protesters are planning to gather outside the Brooklyn home of US Sen. Chuck Schumer on Friday morning, demanding he block what they’ve dubbed a “dirty data center deal” from passing through the Senate. The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), is aimed at speeding the permitting process for energy infrastructure, including renewable energy projects, transmission lines, oil and gas pipelines, and other major industrial developments. The Senate is preparing for a procedural vote on Monday to advance the bill, which will require Democratic support. Schumer (D-NY)—who is hoping to be reelected as Senate majority leader by his party next month—has not publicly taken a position on the legislation, according to Heatmap. The bill has faced opposition from environmental justice and Indigenous rights groups who warn it will gut long-standing environmental protections, undermine tribal sovereignty, and fast-track fossil fuel and other polluting projects, while restricting the public’s ability to challenge harmful developments in court. They warn that the legislation would also accelerate the expansion of energy-hungry artificial intelligence data centers and the gas-fired power plants and pipelines needed to power them, while making it harder for state and local communities to block or challenge their development. Specifically, the bill would expand the authority of the Republican-controlled Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which is chaired by an appointee of President Donald Trump, to approve permits for interstate transmission lines. Jeremy Symons of the Environmental Protection Network has warned that under the BAAJA, the commission could hypothetically issue permits to Elon Musk to build a coal-powered data center in the Grand Canyon and “no one can do anything” about it. The bill was introduced in September in the Senate by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-Utah), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Whitehouse, the bill’s lead Democratic sponsor and the ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, holds the most investments of any US senator in data center-related holdings—between $2.1 million and $8.6 million, according to Forbes. According to Sludge, he and his wife hold up to $12.3 million in AI-related stocks, including major tech companies and data center operators. In a letter sent Thursday, Food & Water Watch and more than 160 other environmental, health, consumer, and religious groups urged Congress to reject the BAAJA. “Data centers can have impacts beyond the lands they occupy, driving significant energy demand and need for grid infrastructure, which can increase cost for the public, as well as create new sources of air and water pollution, which can adversely impact public health and the climate crisis,” they wrote. “This push to expand data centers comes as lawmakers in Washington, DC, are considering a backroom deal that will drive forward a massive buildout of AI data centers and the fossil fuel infrastructure to power them.” Activists with Food & Water Watch, New York Communities for Change, 350Brooklyn, Climate Families NYC, and Indivisible Brooklyn plan to gather outside Schumer’s Park Slope apartment on Friday with a large, smoking AI data center prop and a giant “blank check.” With signs that read “No blank checks for Big Tech” and “stop the dirty data center deal,” they plan to continue the protest afterward at the Fort Greene office of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), who is currently the front-runner to become the next speaker of the House. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), who has proposed banning data centers on federal lands and vocally opposed the BAAJA, noted that the bill would be brought to the floor just days after voters across the country sent “a clear message that Americans want their representatives to protect their health and environment, not sell them out to Big Tech and Big Oil.” On Tuesday, communities across 10 US states passed 43 out of 44 initiatives that proposed banning or pausing construction on data centers or infrastructure of a certain size. Meanwhile, candidates who made opposition to data centers central to their campaigns, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, and Troy Jackson in Maine, won convincingly over their Republican opponents. “People across the country are rightfully chasing data centers out of their communities, and the industry is eyeing public lands as a way around this growing opposition,” said Jim Walsh, policy director at Food & Water Watch. He said that the lawmakers pushing for the BAAJA were doing so “in blatant disregard for the overwhelming public backlash to Big Tech that helped drive voters to the polls.”
